blocks.x: I'll start it out formally by saying we're recording today at 731 St. Peter Street, Donald Russell's record shop, home of American Music Records. What's today's date?
4th of July. It's Armstrong's birthday. Look out for the bird.
It's really Armstrong's birthday. What's your name? Charlie DeVore. And yours?
Ed Lewis.

I'm Dick Allen. Okay, what are we going to talk about today? How to learn how to play New Orleans jazz and how to set up a school, we hope, some sort of thing where we can have seminars and private lessons or what have you, and set up a band. What are your ideas on this, Charlie? You've had some experience.

Well, I don't know exactly what you want, but... Neither do we. If you're just interested in the band aspect as opposed against the individual aspect, there's a few simple little things that can be done to make it pretty fundamental. Now, I think, from my own experience anyway, you've got to have one or two guys with fairly sharp ears if you're going to learn the various tunes. And for musicians that aren't from New Orleans and haven't heard the tunes, the only way they can pick them up is from records, of course. And you have to take melody and the chords from the records. That's where you start. And you've got anybody that can't play. Explain that. I say you have to take the melodies of the tunes and the chords from the tunes probably off the records, even if a guy couldn't play anything. I mean, that's where you'd have to start. And then, once you got the chords... Well, take a simple tune, for instance. Just the blues. That's the way we did it. The fellas that I ran into in Minneapolis were reading these Dixonland arrangements from books, you know. The books that you can buy in New York. They're published in New York. All these fancy Dixonland arrangements. And most of them, they had some experience in reading, but they never tried to muck you around faking it or just ear music. So what I did was show the piano player the very basic blues chords, you know. Tonic and subdominant and dominant and tonic. And then we went from there. Told them just to whack it out four beats to the bar for 12 bars of blues. And I played a simple blues line, and I told the trombone player just to fill in basically what the piano player would be doing in his left hand. And then I told the clarinet player to start playing eighth notes. This is just a very basic beginning without any of the embellishments of jazz music in there. Just running eighth notes from the top of the scale down and back up again to get the driving feeling that the New Orleans clarinetists do. It's a lot more complex than that, but basically that's what they're doing. And we did that for a blues tune and then ran across another tune they might know and did basically the same thing, but over 16 bars or 32 bars on that order. But that was the basic thing for us. We'd get the piano player to sit down in front of the piano and just beat out four beats to the bar. Just bonk, bonk, bonk, bonk, bonk. And then work the trombone part and the clarinet part around that. Of course it goes without saying that the cornet man or the trumpet man would have to know the melody and play it just about as straight as possible. It would sound awfully square at first, and it's not until you get the basic ideas of what has to be done first before you can start putting in some of the other things. And of course it would take guys that had some knowledge of music you've got to have some basic fundamentals even for your music. I think somebody like Raymond Burke, he can hear chords. He doesn't have any idea what the names of the chords or anything else, but he hears the notes in the chords. But there's only one Raymond Burke around. It would be a lot easier for a guy to learn chords. All the front linemen as well as a piano player. Well, Raymond sat down and fooled around with guitars and piano. Oh yeah, sure. He hears the sounds. He's self-taught and he's heard the sounds, but if you'd ask Raymond to hit an E-flat seventh, he would know what you're talking about, you see. But for other guys, this is a shortcut. Raymond's picked this up over a period of years, 30, 35 years of just woodshedding, so to speak. But for a bunch of young guys, I know that's what got me starting to write track. I went over to Johnny Wig's house every Sunday afternoon for about three or four months, and all he did was just show me chords.
On your horn?

Yeah, on the horn. On the horn, yeah. And if you listen to Bunk, you know that he's extremely well-versed in chords. A cornet isn't a chord instrument. When I'm talking about chords, I'm playing all the notes in a chord. Like playing a major chord. Even broken chords. Yeah, running the notes in a chord. Yeah. Oops, I think somebody's trying to break it. Yeah, wait a second.
Well, we're talking about chords now.

Yeah, well, I'll just finish it up briefly on chords. These are just, it kind of starts at the beginning. These are the basic things you have before you start thinking about style or anything else. And it would be wonderful for all the musicians to have a complete training in classical music. Real, complete, legitimate training. All the New Orleans, contrary to popular belief, did. From the TOs, and of course this is all rehash of old stuff. But from all the men that you've interviewed and from the guys that I've talked to, they would maybe have two years of ear training before they ever picked their instrument. You mean somebody like Kid Thomas? No, not Kid Thomas. Some of them. But Kid Thomas, he went through the whole Arben book, played it his own way, of course. Can you imagine Arben being like, wah! I didn't know he would do the Arben method. Sure, sure. Went through the Arben method? Yeah, the whole thing from top to bottom. Manuel Mineta showed me the book he used. He's still got it. All the markings, all the Fess's markings and stuff. Yeah. But, and Thomas can, he can read too. He can read better than I can. Because I've seen him do it. Some guy come up with some sheet music on the job with the tip-top clover of specs and want to play some corny thing. And they put the sheet music on it and he read it. I think maybe he was spelling it more than he was reading it, but that's still better than I can do. But I still think that for a bunch of young guys, these are all shortcuts. The New Orleans men, the type of music they played covered a great period of years. Trial and error. Well, like Raymond, for instance. He's the one I can think of offhand because he's almost in the classic New Orleans way of doing things. Getting to a spot and getting stuck and then figuring out his own shortcut from his own sheer genius or intellect, whatever you want to call it. But I was pointing out the basic things. The cornet player, the lead man to learn the melodies, the piano man to learn the right changes, and for the other men, regardless of what instrument they have, to know chords.
Do you think that it would help if every guy took piano in the back?

Yeah, absolutely. Couldn't go wrong. Keep more harmony? Yeah, this process speeds things up. And then, you see, for New Orleans things, and this is the hardest thing, the modern guys could play New Orleans jazz if they wanted to, but the hardest thing to do is to funnel all this background and training into a very simple form of music and discipline yourself. That is where all the guys playing these days that aren't really saying much are having troubles because they don't realize the amount of discipline this music takes. They're strained. Yeah, that's right. Because they've had all this training and they have the technique, they can whip off just by anything they please. But it takes somebody with quite a bit of discipline to be able to play the New Orleans style right. Now, as an example, I heard a record by Pee Wee Irwin of the New York Cats and a fellow by the name of Dick Carey who is an accomplice musician you'd want to meet. And he plays alto horn, you know, peck horn, and other instruments too. Yeah. But in this particular, they decided they were going to make some George Lewis records. And they did. And he was thumping out, here's a classic kick-train piano going, whap, whap, whap, whap, whap. Dick Carey. With Lou McGarty and those guys. And you could tell it was much more polished and didn't have the real punch. But still, it kind of approximated the sound. I'm not saying everybody has to be a completely finished musician before they can play. That's ridiculous. But these things going back before you start worrying about New Orleans music are important. And a guy that has these things is much better off because it's not so hard for him. Well, how does he get rid of the polish, though? Well, now, this goes into the other end of listening to the records, of course, if you don't have a musician's area. But, of course, the best thing of all is having New Orleans musicians that you can listen to live. And you have to start with somebody. I don't care who you are. Armstrong started out playing maybe play like Bunk, probably more like Joe Oliver than anything else. He tried to. And anybody would have to pick somebody that they admired tremendously. And not exactly copy the style, but try and approximate all the things that the guy did. And you have to start somewhere. And then you can develop your own voice and your own style from there. But that's kind of getting ahead of it. So those are the basic things to start out with. You got that. And then from there, once you got those down, the piano player with the right chords and the cornet player playing the lead. Those are the first two things. And now the next is for the trombone and the clarinet player to voice within the trombone player roughly approximating the left hand of the piano and the clarinet roughly approximating the right hand of the piano like Jelly. Jelly style of the piano playing, which is band style. Playing all the instruments in the band. The piano covers the whole thing, really. You listen to Jelly Roll, you can hear a whole band. But it's that basic thing. Well, what about
brass band style? Do you think that has any influence on the band style?

Yeah. Oh, yeah, absolutely. But you hear the same things in a brass band style. The trombone player hitting a solid foundation, which would approximate the left hand. And then the cornet man playing the melody. And then the reed man filling in and embellishing. But for the filling in and embellishing part, it's very simple, like I said before, for a clarinet man just to start with eighth notes. Take the key of the tune you're playing in and just run a circle of eighth notes just going up and down the scale. That's all you have to do to start with it to get the feeling of it. And for a trombone player to be hitting on one and three. Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Boom, boom, boom. Something real basic like that. And then you start and then you take it from there. The rest of it would have to be from listening to records and actually listening to New Orleans men. Well, how do you get that rhythm?
I mean, there certainly is a definite rhythm.
Well, yeah. And do you get that from records or do you get that
from studying with a guy or do you get it from sitting in or what?

Well, for a New Orleans style band, the most important thing as far as rhythm is concerned is you're playing four-four time rather than two beat or any other times that bands have played. And the rhythm angle is the most important of all. I mean, even if a guy couldn't play a lick on a piano or a cornet, just make a few notes if he did it with punch. That would represent more jazz feeling than a guy that could rip off a whole slew of notes and stuff from the strictly legitimate end. So you aim for punch, huh? Yeah.
What's punch? How do these guys get that punch is what I'm getting at?
Well,
it's obviously not just unaccented four-four.

No. They have to do other things on top of that. Well, the punch, of course, the rhythm section is the most basic of all as far as the front line is concerned. That's what they lean on. That's the foundation. I'm not even talking about drumming right now because that's so complex and that's what makes and breaks a band is the drumming. But let's put it this way. The classical setup of a band is three-four rhythm, actually, and three front line and sometimes four if you have two cornets, two trumpets. But for a rhythm section, to be playing four-four, is the start of it, the foundation. And then these other things that the men are doing, the trombone playing the bass pedal parts and the coronet playing the lead. Our bass player, he's a pretty sharp boy. He said that on the listening that he's done, that the three things that may, I don't care what instrument you play or what you're doing, there's three things that have to be there before I have a real jazz feeling. And that's a tack, tonality, and, let's see, what was the other one? Can you think of?
The melody.
Yeah. The only thing it has to be, but it has to be varied. Yeah.
Improvised.

Well, anything. I mean, the way a guy goes about doing something, I mean, like, for instance, a guy lombardo man can come in and play the melody straight. You know, a guy lombardo man could come in and play the melody straight, but why wouldn't it be jazz? Because he hasn't got the attack and he hasn't got the tonality. What is tonality? And he hasn't got the phrasing. Yeah, that's the three things. Phrasing, attack, and tonality.
Yeah, but what is tonality?

Well, the tonality is the tone that a man makes on his horn. It's very easy for a person that's acquainted with jazz at all to hear a straight man and a hot man play exactly the same thing. You say, well, this is jazz and the other thing is, well, it's nice, but it's not really jazz. And attack is a way you hit the first notes of your phrases. And phrasing is essentially how far off the beat you can play and still retain the melody.
Right, that's the thing.

That is, that's where most white, like, for instance, the Blue Water School, the West Coast School of traditional jazz, that all seemed to me to be something they missed. They all came down to beat at the same time. The tonality was there, I always liked Lou Waters playing. He seemed to get a hot tone, but when he, his phrasing always sounded stiff to me because they were always going plump, plump, plump right on the beat. And all the good guys, the guys that I've admired the most and to me that play the most jazz, always had the phrasing that was off the beat. And I didn't realize that myself while I was down here. That's something that never was explained to me. I didn't realize it until I was playing out of Doc Evans' place up in Mendota, Minnesota. And we were playing and Doc Evans came up to me and said, gee, why don't you play a little bit more off the beat? I think it would help. And when he said that, I realized that that was where I was having so much trouble.
you were coming down right on the beat.

Right on the beat. I don't know if it's a natural thing for white musicians or not. Color musicians seem to instinctively play against the beat. Before or after all. Yeah. White musicians instinctively seem to hit at the same time. Well, you yourself can tell if you watch the people over that preservation hall. They're all stomping the foot. They understand that. And when they clap, they clap on the beat. One and three. Maybe a musician wouldn't, but the majority of the people, whenever you hear people clapping if they're white, they're on one and three almost invariably. And that's another form of being on the beat, so to speak.
Well, I notice that when I'm with a crowd of white people that I tend to clap on one and three, you know.
That's because they do.
They do. But if I'm with colored people, you know, say at a parade, well, then I feel the two and four much more. You know, I'm more relaxed around them or something
and it comes more easily to me. Yeah, well, these are all things that a band has to keep in mind and it's a job
and it doesn't take, it takes a lot of work. But when you say off the beat, do you mean two and four or do you mean like bumping, holding back a little?

Yeah, that's what I mean, holding back. Phrasing, see. Phrasing off the beat. A whole phrase off the beat. In other words, you could start ahead, you end up behind. Play behind, play ahead. Like Louie, see, he, on this tune once in a while, his little instrument goes, he goes, they start out one, two, one, two, see, he holds back and holds and I mentioned that Louie thing because that little introduction always knocked me out. Yeah, well, Louie perhaps did it more than anybody but Joe Oliver, in some respects was even more subtle than Armstrong, the things that I've heard, more shading and stuff. So much of that was involved in how he phrased. Phrasing, attack, and tonality. That's the three things I keep in my mind whenever I play. No matter what. If I take some strange tunes, maybe some pop tune that might be popular right now that somebody requests and we try and play it. I have to do that sometimes, you know, every New Orleans band runs into that to make it hot so it won't sound like some other square playing, you've got to keep the three things in mind. Keep the... Now when I say tonality, I might expound upon that a little bit more. It's the vibrato. That is what gives a man a hot sound as opposed to a legitimate man straight tone. It's the vibrato. You can't... When I talk to, well, like our clarinet players maybe when it's two months, that's all I tell them to do when he plays. Work on that vibrato. Get it so it practically shakes your horn to pieces. Over-emphasize it at first and after a while you can get it so you can control it. Every man's got to have that. That's what gives you the hot sound. A vibrato, a legitimate vibrato is in all the books, you can find in all the books shaking the horn against your lip. I myself do it with my lip. I don't know, just naturally. Do you shake your jaw? I shake my chops, yeah.
Shake your bottom jaw

like that, huh? And a clarinet man is the same thing, exactly the same way. Our first clarinet man, Dick Ramberg, he had a lot of trouble with that so I kept after him to shake because I'd seen Raymond do that and I'd seen George too. And you know, it's not vibrato all the time. Kid Thomas plays, well, no, he puts, the vibrato is usually at the end of a phrase. It holds a note and shakes it. Yeah, you hold a note and at the end you shake it, you know. But you can have it going in the middle part too but it's most pronounced at the end. That's how the New Orleans musicians get that cracking sound. I'm thinking of Hormann particularly but the other men too.
Well, how do they crack it? Now, explain that again. In the middle of a phrase?

No, at the end, at the end. It's by emphasizing the vibrato, I always think of the vibrato in terms of wavelength. Up and down wavelength and getting more frequent as you get toward the end of a phrase. Kind of shake, either shaking a horn or using your chops and a trombone man the same way. Yeah, a trombone man uses a vibrato like Jim.
Yeah, but he uses slide partly some of them.
Well, he'd slide and lift. Yeah. Like the real old time
was I noticed they used slide much more.
Yeah, right.
Like say Louie Nelson
uses his chops
and the modern guys
didn't use the vibrato.
Louie uses his

combination of well, the trombone man it's a combination of slide and your chops. Like Jim, when he'll hit a long note he'll go like that and he does that with his lip. But then Louie when he hits something he goes he shakes the slide moves the slide back and forth as fast as he can. And Ori and our trombone player that's how we worked on his vibrato by using the slide. That's how you get that nice tone. See a trombone is the only instrument in the band that can do it that way because he has a slide. Well now do you think this is all

involved in tonality though? If we're going to set up some sort of little school or something do you think how do you think we should start? Do you think we should start with individual lessons from an old musician to a young guy or should it be the band or what or both or everything? Well the way I see it

you'd have to the musicians that you'd have to start up on an individual basis it would be possible to take a man perhaps who didn't have any musical background or experience and just wanted to understand the philosophy that went into the music. That's one end. But from a strict playing end to me it always would seem that the most ideal setting would be a band setting because from a band angle I think a person can appreciate the give and take of New Orleans music much more than from an individual angle. To me the beauty of New Orleans music was collective improvisation and because of that I've always believed that the band is more important than the individual. The good of the band and the ability to be able to play with other men because you yourself know when you get a bunch of all stars together they could be just great individually in their instruments and really good men on their instruments from a jazz standpoint but they couldn't play together. It always meant more to me to be able to have it from a band angle so that's what I would say. And then to start out like I said before the chords the melody the trombone way of doing things and the clarinet way of doing things which I described earlier. And then I should explain this because a good band is a three rhythm or a three or four rhythm in the three front lines so you'd have the drumming and the bass. Now I didn't mention much about the drums before. For a drummer to start out we're taking everything this for granted that the men if you wanted a man to do something on his instrument he could do it because he had some previous background experience maybe not experience but a training on his instrument and that would hold true for all the men. all that taken for granted then you would start out with your band. And I mentioned the other instruments now a drumming that can be broken on quite simply too. Four four on the bass drum because that's the easiest to understand. Snare press rolls those two things. All a man would have to have is a bass drum and a snare drum. Where does he play the press roll? He plays the press rolls on two and four. Now a press roll I'm not a drummer myself I can't exactly explain it.
We've got that explained by other people.

You've got that explained by other people. Okay everybody knows what a press roll is. Well these press rolls are played on two and four. The bass drum is played four and four. So you've got syncopation. Right. You've got the two things that's supposed to. And that would be the very basic thing. Now you have the bass player. That's going to be broken out very simply too. The bass player would play the two notes of the chord that the I'll take a simple tune. In one bar he would play usually the tonic and the dominant. Now a guy who knows music would know what I'm talking about when I'm saying the tonic and the dominant notes of every chord in the tune. Two beats to each bar. First and the fifth. First and the fifth. Yeah. So you have like a simple spiritual like a close walkly. And this also represents the left hand of the piano player. And something a bass player has to understand is that you have four beats to the bar and you do not ever play a third on a strong beat. Never play a third. A third of a chord on a strong beat. That's just that is a law of the bass players. They might not be aware of it but that for a good it's just any good bass player always never plays a third on a strong beat. You use a third in a passing type of thing. that type of thing. But it was see he wouldn't he could play a third because a third was in the chord but if he did it would sound very weak. and that's that is the basic thing for a bass man to do. And that's also four four although he can play one and three but this is the very basic stuff. You would get a very basic beginning New Orleans sound if you had the men doing that. If you had the piano player playing four four on the chords the drummer hitting the bass drum four beats press rolls and the bass player doing what I just described. The cornet player melody and the clarinet player running the eighth notes and the trombone player roughly playing the same thing that the bass is playing and the piano and the string bass. That would you beginning to get the very beginning New Orleans sound. We're planning to
use Paul Crawford I guess I told you
how because you teach it because he knows music. He knows it from both angles he really knows all kinds of jazz and knows legitimate.
I think it would be helpful to have somebody who's taught all instruments.

Oh absolutely you couldn't go wrong. I mean I would be so much better off with the men in our band if I knew music because I really don't you know. These are things that have come about not just from me but from the other guys in the band too and from listening to records and from talking to the guys who just know music in general. But that would be the basic setup for a band and then you work. That was the very first thing that you would establish. You wouldn't have to have any tunes at all. Just one tune. Just take maybe a simple blues in different tempos. Slow blues and medium fast blues. That seems to be the most simple way of doing things. That's the way we did it. Then we would start to get a New Orleans song. Do you kind of understand what I mean? Is there anything that you have any question about? That's for the basic. Then you go from there as far as the actual assimilation of the New Orleans music itself is concerned.
Say we've got Paul setting them up like that. What about having guest lecturers?

That's invaluable because for instance you have maybe Jim Robinson come by. He hears the band and you've set the band up and you've got this so far. You've got a blues going medium tempo and you've got everybody doing this. Very simple and it would be very stiff. Then you slip Jim in there and say Jim this is with the band. What would you do playing along with us? The tromboman would drop out and Jim would start playing and he was going all the things that Jim does. Then a tromboman could really begin to get some understanding of these things. Probably after you got this down regardless of what kind of tone you use or what kind of attack you use then you could work on the tonality and the attack and the phrasing. The only way that a guy can really understand that is by listening to the New Orleans men on record or having them right there. That's what you would need a man on the job for to be a New Orleans man to come in and help you. That's where you could utilize his he wouldn't have to explain anything. All he had to do was just play because if the man you had in your band was playing a simple melody like you tell me your dream and he knew the melody straight through then you'd have maybe another man the trumpet man like Kid Thomas come in and he played the way he plays it and then he could tell the way Tom's tonality the type of tone he gets and he could ask Tom how he did this and the way Tom phrased and he could also ask him about that and Tom most likely could be able to answer them. I was thinking the New Orleans men would be able to teach in this respect from demonstration in the same way with clarinet men. Well I think
that some of the New Orleans guys are pretty good talkers too.

Oh absolutely. Yeah. Not only from the musical and from the philosophy and that's just as important as anything else. I mean being able to get along with your fellow man that seems to be the most important thing of all. When there's a bad feeling running in the band you're not going to play as good music. I found that out from bitter experience. So no matter how good a guy is and if you're not getting along you're not going to be able to come up with a real New Orleans feeling. Very, very few bands would be able to overcome the personal conflict angle. The bands that were able to overcome were the ones that stuck together the longest and played probably the best collective improvisation.
There's a philosophy of playing in a band and understanding
your role
and understanding who you are in relation to the other people. At least to me it seems to me. Even though it's never spoken sometimes.
Yeah, it never has to
be spoken. Like we were
talking about Albert Warner and Sonny Henry. Crazy. You say, you guys good buddies? They probably say, oh, I don't know, he's kind of a no good SOB. Kidding me. But you knew that they were always
together and

bummed together. Sure. And that's just as those two things from a strictly musical angle and from a strictly getting along angle. Very important. As anybody who's ever played in a jazz band can tell you. Well, say
we have Paul teaching these guys and I think he would know how to give them a legitimate approach. He would know how to give
them a jazz approach. If a guy
has an idea, would it help him to go take lessons from his idea?

Yeah, sure. I don't see why not. That's the idea I had. And a lot of times the lessons wouldn't be involved with playing the instrument at all. Just talking. Talking to them. Understanding maybe the kind of life they led. This all goes into New Orleans music. Who did you go and talk to? Well, the guys that I talked the most to are Kid Punch and Kid Thomas and Manuel Mineta and Johnny Wiggs. I think those are the four guys I spent the most amount of time with. Of the trumpet men, you know. Although Mineta teaches all instruments. And besides those men for just talking about music in general, just being around New Orleans musicians helps a guy to play better. I think because their terrific philosophy of life.
Well, I
think it gives you confidence. Absolutely. If you're young, you're
around those men, they have confidence in what they can do. They know their message.
They have tremendous pride. The thing that's underlying all that, it may not be quite the...

All right, let's see. We're talking about how these men have pride in what they've done. Well, they have a tremendous amount of pride. It's not exactly on the surface, you know, and they'll kid around and bark to music like Jim, you know, it seems like he's clowning around everything, but when you get right down to brass tacks, man, these men love music and they have a tremendous amount of pride in their, in the way that they do things. All the New Orleans men have. That's the thing that struck me after I got to know them for a while. It wouldn't, they'd be almost, it seems to me when I first met them.
This is rail 3 of Charlie DeVore. July 4, 1962 it is.

Yeah, well I want to just talk a little bit about the individual instruction from the New Orleans guys. Now, we had a session Sunday afternoon, which is the 1st of July, and we played a tune called Climax Rag, which is quite popular with Percy and George Lewis's band played a little bit. And Jim likes that tune a lot, and after when we got through... Howard too. Oh yeah, Howard plays it great. He plays all his own stuff in there. But afterwards Jim came up to me and said, hey I heard it. You know how Jim stutters and everything. What are you saying man? Yeah. What's best?
What's best Charlie?

Yeah, that's it. He said, man I heard that Climax Rag, you know. He says, you like that tune. And he said, we played it all the time. He said, I heard you steal that from me. That's what he said anyway. But he said, it's a trombone partner that you didn't play. And he was talking to a trombone man. And he sang it to him, see. And Rusty didn't get it the first time around. He's like me, it takes about 20 times around and doesn't really get it. But then once he gets it, he usually remembers it. And it's things like that that you can pick up on an individual basis. Where you hear a tune and maybe there's a real way of doing it that to do it this way, you're not exactly copying. If you didn't do it this way, it wouldn't be really the tune, you see. And Jim had that trombone part that he was singing to Rust. I've heard him do it on the records and it's on there every time. And you see, Rust didn't do it when we were playing it. So Jim thought that he would show them and sing it to him. So he'd pick it up so we'd play. He said, that's part of the tune. And the last night we were talking about it. And he said, well, there's not too much for a trombone to do on that. In a way something's really distinctly trombone. Jim wasn't, yeah, you know how Jim talks. But that's what he was getting at. And so when you come up with something like that, it's nice to play those things. And he went over it with Rust and sang it a couple of times. And I remember, as soon as he started singing it, I remember having heard it on Bill's, the climax sessions at the tea room. And then, I don't know, I told Jim that I thought he played it great on the Hup record, but nobody's heard the Hup record down here.
It was down here but not much. Yeah. I know.
You have it. Yeah, that's uh, that's a... That's a... That's a Swans catalog.
I thought they cut it off.
This wasn't some guy in Florida. Well, he was on the Hup. Jim couldn't remember the Hup session at all. Well, that's 12 years ago. Yeah. Oh yeah, absolutely.
Well, not only that, he probably didn't know it was being recorded.
Yeah, I think that was the date.
Yeah, it was made at a concert.

Yeah. Auditorium, yeah. So he pointed that out, you know. And like on Climax Ragnar, you've got to play it that way. And if you take the sheet music, I heard a piano transcription of that tune and listened to the melody on there and followed that real close. But you see, a New Orleans guy wouldn't do it exactly the way it was written. And that's what a young guy could pick up individually.
Well, I noticed Thomas, you know, when you played his tune?
Yeah, we played it too fast.
That's what he said.

Yeah. That's something else too old. Gee, that's so important. God, how could I forget that? Temples. New Orleans bands never play anything very fast. Racehorse tempo. And that's the beauty of it. That's why the drumming's so important in New Orleans band because you've got, the temples are much more moderate because the bands are always played for dancing. That's the way I figured it. And like Tom says too, you can get, you don't have to worry so much about making fast runs if fingering and that type of thing. And you can think of more tasty things to do. That's what he said in essence. And ordinarily, we do play Aldris Drutt slower, but our drummer has a tendency to drag. He only has one or two temples he can play. We start out a slow tune, real slow, like a slow drag him out blues. He'll pick up the tempo until he gets it where he's used to playing it. And the same way with the moderate tunes. That's why the drumming's so damn important. God, I can't stress that enough. A guy could, I've spent more time studying drums than I have cornet, particularly lately. Because a guy, a drummer makes or breaks it. And tempo, I mean, timekeeping, man, that is the most basic fundamental of all. But so many young drummers, they can't keep time. And that's why the best bands down here sound the best because the drummer keeps a pretty accurate time.
What about the sense of meter, Charlie? How do you get at that?

Well, the meter in music, that's in all kinds of music. That's something, if a guy hasn't got a sense of meter, he can't play. It's impossible. And I think that goes along with a guy's either got an ear for music or he hasn't. There's plenty of people that just don't have an ear for music. I mean, you sing something to them and they try and sing it back, they can't. And this is a physical defect more than anything else. And meter is right along with it. Like, well, when you're singing, he wouldn't say, you tell me your dream. I mean, you know, you're just singing along, but you're not analyzing what you're doing when you're doing it. But some guy might, you tell me your dream, oh, tell you my, you know, he's jumping around. I remember I heard Raymond play with the most horrible band once and the trumpet player was doing that. He'd be finished before anybody else was. That's meter. Jumping out and that's closely connected with phrasing. But it's all these time values. If he had it written out, he couldn't understand it. But that's what they call meter.
But how do guys learn? Say, you know, you've got a young guy here and he doesn't, he's never thought about meter maybe and he wants to play New Orleans music.

Well, a meter is something that everybody learns from childhood. If I asked Ed to sing a song here, now Ed's isn't a musician, he's never played anything, but he'd sing a song in a proper meter. I don't care what it is. If Ed could sing, how would you sing three blind mice? You'd sing, three blind mice. You'd take a pause there, right?
Three blind mice. I wouldn't bet on it.

No, well, I mean, that's the thing, see? Why did he take the pause? He couldn't tell you. You start singing something, why do you pause there? You couldn't answer it yourself. And that's meter. That's something that you pick up from childhood. You pick up from maybe your mother singing lullabies to you when you're a baby. The people that don't have it, like I said, it's a physical defect.
So you don't think that that can be learned then? I don't think so.

I've been trying, my wife hasn't got any feeling of meter. I've been trying to, she'll play, I've been to take her finger and play one of the saints on the piano. She's been doing that. She'll go, da, da, da, da, da, da. Trouble is, I can't sing out of meter myself. I can't do it. I've tried, you know? But she could do it. And all of a sudden, she'll jump, you know? Instead of holding a note, you know, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da. She won't give the note, holding the notes the proper time.
Yeah, well, I notice, if I'm nervous, I tend to sing out of meter. And if I'm not thinking about it, I'll sing in meter.
Yeah, well,
that's it. I might be nervous that's something to do with it, just getting relaxed in the music, you know?

Yeah. But when you're listening to a band, you can sing right along with them, you know? And you can no more get out of that than the Man of the Moon. Well, if you're by, Yeah, but if you're by yourself, you should be able to do the same thing regardless of the jazz music or anything else. I mean, see, when I say meter, why do you take a pause at the end of a thing? Well, it just seems natural. It would be almost, you couldn't do it any other way. Well, that's meter. And guys, the jump meter is the saying goals there. There was a piano player, he was classically trained and everything else, but doggone, he'd jump meter all the time and drove us absolutely crazy. He just couldn't play. But yet, he was the guy who was completely trained in music. He was trained mechanically. He was taught, when he saw a note, he'd tap out, you'd see a quarter note, one beat, tap out a dotted half note, three beats, one, two, three. He could do that and that way he could play. But take the music away from him, he wouldn't know how long to hold a note before he'd go on the next phrase. And that's where the phrasing comes in, see. But what about silence?
Is that important? What? What about silence then? Is that important? Oh, yeah.

Particularly for a cornet player. You see, when a cornet player is playing a lead, he should play it not abruptly, melodically and smoothly, leaving what I call holes for the other one to fill in. Like, I'm on this You Tell Me Your Dream Jimbo, that's the last tune Jim played last time. You play la, da, la, da, da, and there's a pause there, see. And then the clarinet, do, do, do, do, do, that eighth note thing. And you go la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, But now some trumpet players like Doc Evans for instance, that's all he talks about. Well guys never play straight enough, but Doc will play. He'll play. See, it's going all the time and there's no room.
Well what about the clarinet play? Should he be going all the time?
Yeah, yeah. He'd be driving on. He doesn't have to do it.
He doesn't have to phrase it.

See, here's the way for ensemble, which is the most important thing and it's the hardest to get the integration of the front line. To integrate, you have the clarinet play going here and basically this is what amounts to. He plays a straight lead and when the holes come, the clarinet fills in and the trombone fills in. And you can have a lamellia line here with a fill in line starting here and back and forth. A Dixieland style is very cut and dried, like a Phil Napoleon band. When the clarinet player stops, the clarinet player starts. When the clarinet player stops, the clarinet player starts. It's all like this. But New Orleans style, you have a clarinet player here and maybe he'll start here, start here, start here, anywhere. The clarinet might start at any point.
Yeah.

But of course, and it's taken for granted, he'll be playing when the clarinet player drops out. Like the Thomas band, Thomas plays the straightest lead of anybody in town. More so than a person, anybody. Short, hot notes. With the biggest gaping holes. And then the guys are always filling in like Manuel Paul or Louis Nelson. But a clarinet player, the silence angle is extremely important because he's got to drop out so there's room for the other men. So you have the band sound rather than just a bunch of individuals playing. That's why an all-star band sounds bad. Not in all instances, you know. But when I'm thinking of the popular conception of an all-star band, a bunch of guys are whiz-bangs on their instruments. Everybody playing all at once. I've heard Doc Evans' band play when it's knock your ear drums down. Because everybody just go in the town all at once and there's no holes. So where you've got things switching back and forth between trombone, clarinet, and trumpet.
But this goes back to the conception of discipline and form.

Discipline and form, yeah. Well that's it. That's why New Orleans music is such a disciplined music. Because you've got to force yourself. Particularly if you've got the technique to do anything you want to do. Then you've got to discipline yourself and force yourself to do these things. To play the style. You wouldn't have to do that but then you're not playing real New Orleans styles.
What's the place of harmony in a band?

Well, now you, this is a pretty involved thing. You see now, the bands that are playing today are, if you were looking over the whole history of New Orleans music, these are the seconds, so to speak. The real top notch professional New Orleans men had everything these guys did besides working on arrangements like the Oliver Band for instance. They say the Oliver Band down here must have really been something. A lot more fluid than the band that recorded in Chicago. But if you listen to that band in Chicago, they had tunes that had two or three different strains. Breaks. You see, Jelly Roll knew more about it than anybody. He was a guy at that time that understood what was going on. I think Joe did too, but Jelly really did. And it's the breaks that mean so much. And for harmonies, well you listen to Working Man Blues by Oliver Band. And every band is playing a different part at the same time harmonized out. You can hear the two horns. Louie is playing a harmonic part underneath the lead. The trombone player has this part. The clarinet player has this part. And we do a lot of that. We call it three part, very basic three part harmonies. Ori's band. Now there's a band, the classic Ori band, the one with Papa Mutt. And two or three of the good clarinet players. Orma Simeon or Darnell Howard. And Ori, with that wonderful rhythm section. I think that band probably, of the modern bands, came as close as being the real polished New Orleans. With the same amount, the roughness was still there, but the organization was as polished as any band.
Do you know who I think was responsible for a lot of that?
Well, certainly the rhythm section was together and good.
Oh yeah. But I think the guy in the front line, that changed the sonority of the band through his tonal shading, his Mutt.
Oh yeah.
Because that guy, he was in every chorus, he varies his tone.

Yeah, I can't, and his phrasing too. Yeah, there's a guy that I think is extremely underrated. I talked to some of the Whiteman, and he said, oh he has such a bad tone. Well, Mutt's tone wasn't like the other guys, but it was hot. And his phrasing was excellent, and he could really finger that instrument too, you know. Yeah, Mutt was just great. Well, I think that many of the white guys don't like vibrato. I love vibrato, and I love Mutt. Mutt had a very wide vibrato. Yeah, I've always liked Mutt. I think Mutt with the Ori band, and the things that Mutt made with Jimmy Archie and Edmund Hall are just wonderful. Can't talk about them enough. There's a guy I know he pays any attention to. I listen to Mutt as much as I have anybody else. Well, it's obvious the English fans do. Yeah.
You listen to them, you know that they really study it.

Yeah. Poor Mutt, he's really taken a beating through the jazz history and stuff. But he was a guy who could really play. That Ori band was really a wonderful band. They had all the things that the white musicians complain about when they hear the rougher bands. Man, they made changes, they made it all. Ori was a damn good trombone player. He was a tough guy to work for though, from all the reports that I've heard. Don Ewell particularly, probably things about his personality. But boy, he was a musical taskmaster and knew what he wanted. And they worked on those harmony parts. Very, like you take, let's see, what's one of those things? Yeah. Oh, the record I like best of is this one that's called, this tailgate put off by Good Time Jazz. They have 1919, Diddy Ramble.
I like the part he plays when all the whores like to obey our rights. Yeah. That's a beautiful part, the way they have that worked out in the band.
Yeah.

One thing I think about it, even in the harmony choruses, New Orleans' guys- Rough. Always rough. And they exploit the natural phrasing of their instrument instead of them trying to be quite together. Right. It's not quite unison. And something about that, it's a very loose unison.

I don't know. Well, not unison. Yeah. The parts, the good ones, you know, this is what I'm trying to assume. Like George's band, see, they're used to playing the strict ensemble style with lone harmony parts and everything, and it's catch as catch can. Yeah. Which is a kind of an intermediate style between the early Bowlin style and the finished full-time professionalism of an Armstrong, an Ori, or an Oliver, you know. Mm-hmm. That's where these bands kind of fall in between. Like I say, they were the second-liners. It's a casual band. Yeah. They were kind of the second-liners at the time these other men were playing, because the other men were older, too.
Mm-hmm.

And there's really a distinguishing part. Like, that's the criticism that I hear so many of us. So the guys that admire the Oliver band and Louie's Hot Fives and Sevens don't care for George Lewis, because, well, I said, those were their interpretation of the real Rollins guys, and when the other bands are lacking changes and stuff, they're criticizing tremendously. Of course, I'm always fighting that battle up there, too, but that's another story. But that's where the harmonies work in. And yet, you take a harmony like Doc Evans, when his band plays the harmonies, it sounds like a baroque quartet, you know. Mm-hmm. But yet Ori would do the same thing with the same voice in the instruments. They retain the vibrato, and their attack is along the jazz lines. Not exactly on the beat, see. And not quite together.
Mm-hmm.

And when we play, I never like to get myself, even on the harmony parts, I like to change it around as much as possible. Even just the accents. You can still play together, but change the accents around, and it makes it sound interesting. But all those Oliver tunes had them worked out. I like working man blues. And they were like, oh, you know, you can hear. And the breaks and stuff. That was all harmony parts. And then the most classic part in that whole tune, Richard M. Jones wrote that tune. They had the horns, the cornet, and the trombone, two cornets, and the trombone. La, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la. That was worked out perfectly harmonically. The trombone player played a third above the two horns coming down. And Riverside Blues the same way. So those are the guys that were the very so-called the cream of the crop of the New Orleans men. Guys that had evolved themselves full-time professionally and had a complete knowledge of music more so than, say, like Jim. And that's where that came in. But I think a young band would do well to absorb all these different styles from all the good New Orleans bands that have played. From Oliver to Jellie Roll. Now there's a guy that just goes to show you what the best New Orleans men could do with arrangements. And look at the wonderful music that came out. It's completely arranged. And that just goes to show you. And that is kind of a stopgap for the guys that say, oh you can't arrange anything New Orleans and make it sound like real New Orleans music. But they did and you can't say it's anything but New Orleans music. And for those same three reasons. Attack, the tone of the instruments, the hot sound, and the phrasing.

Well, I listened to the Ori interview that Naz did. Did you ever hear that one? No. Well, Ori talks about it and he says all that was so beautifully arranged and everything except that he wasn't reading his part. No, Ori knew all that stuff. Ori knew all that stuff. Sure. But some of it was new to him, I'm sure. But he knew it almost immediately. He could just listen and grab it right away somehow. Yeah, Ori... Because he had such an ear, or had such an ear, I don't know. I haven't heard his recent records.

Yeah, no, all his... I haven't heard the more up to date stuff. I've heard some of it. Some of it's very good. Ori has got kind of a contemporary sound to his band. It's fantastic. Ori is really a disciplinarian because he can take the modern cats and make them play the way he wants them to. So his bands, even with modern piano players, have that common Ori sound. I can't understand it. You know, taking guys like Marty Marcella and... Well, Darnell Howard, of course, who always played in the wrong style. But other guys, and yet get kind of the same sound. I have an approximation of it. And I think Ori just drove it into them.
Well, what about... Do you think that your band has had any effect on the Minneapolis listening public?

Oh, absolutely. We've gained a following, you know. And now there's two separate schools. There's Doc Evans School and the Hall Brothers School for listening to music. We've been able to convert a lot of people, not because of musicianship, because we're pretty sure on that, actually. In that respect, I think we kind of resemble the bands down here. We've learned just enough music to do what we want to do. And they haven't gone into any really... gone into the pursuit of the instrument very deeply. But just to play the kind of... you know, the real New Orleans guys, they knew all music. Which is right, I think. But there's the time involved and what you want to do with it. I mean, the requirements for a band these days are so much different than they were back in those days. A person would... I think ideally it would be perfect for a person to learn music top to bottom. But for our purposes, it has been adequate to learn just enough music to do what we wanted to do. For harmony parts and things like that. But the audiences respond to our band for the same reason that they respond to a New Orleans band. The rhythmical angle. Rhythm, rhythm, rhythm. We pound that into everybody in the ensembles to back up a man all the time with riffs. With hot riffs. That's where the swing bands got those from New Orleans bands anyway. And rhythm all the time. And that regards if it's an actual rhythm section man or a horn man. A good New Orleans band to me was a six piece rhythm section. That's why I always looked at it. Not always. I mean, that's... That's the way it evolved into this. As far as my own thing is going. The more I can become familiar with the music. That it would seem like the bands that... In this respect, a band made up of some of the New York guys like Wild Bill. I like Wild Bill. He doesn't play a real classic New Orleans style. But he plays hot and he does this backing up and stuff. And some of the things he made with Cindy Bichet were just wonderful. Cindy Bichet and Jimmy Archie.
He's got a fierce attack.

Yeah, that's the thing. See, there is again. Wild Bill, to me, is the most creative of the hot school in New York because of his attack and his tone and his phrasing. When he gets down, it always gets down to those three things.

Well, I hate to put you on the spot and you don't have to answer it. Who would you rather listen to, Jim Robinson or Henri Dutre? Jim Robinson, without a doubt. And so there's something to be said for a guy who's a real talk musician like Jim.

Yes, right. I'm not putting Jim down a bit because he had... Jim, see, it's like I say, he's learned as much music as was necessary for the band. Maybe Jim could only learn so much music, you know. Henri, on the other hand, never had the punch that Jim had. But to me, the more I listened to it, Henri had a very nice style. I'm not so sure that he didn't play quite a bit better live than he did in the records. Because I've heard Armstrong and other guys have played in that band. How many are left alive? I guess Louis is about the only one, isn't he? St. Cyril. Yeah, that's right, St. Cyril. I read an interview by him. They all like Dutre's playing. But they like Dutre's playing a lot. And he got gassed, you know, in the first world war and that he never did play as good after that.
I think one thing is that you listen to him on the Dodge records and you can hear a little better what his style was like. I think he was on a Genet Studio disadvantage.

Right, I think he has a lot to do with it too. But no matter how good he played, I think Jim played with more punch. And of course Jim to me is my favorite trombone player of all time. Because he plays the most punch of any trombone player I've heard on record or in person. And I like that the best. Like I say, Jim's a one-man rhythm section.
Do you think there's anything distinctive about the mechanics of New Orleans playing? How you hold your hands or how you finger?

Well, from my own observation, not particularly. I watch Percy's playing. He fingers his instrument extremely legitimate. Fingers all the way at the tips of his fingers. When he holds his horn and he's using his instrument, he does. But when he's playing and he's holding his horn with his left hand, he's not using the ring, you know. And the classical men don't like rings on horns. Because they say it interferes with the... When you play, see those two fingers go together like that. And that would interfere with the motion. If you held that solid, it would interfere with the motion of your fourth finger there. So I've seen both of them. I've seen some players come all the way over. I don't think there's any particular... I'll tell you one thing distinctive though. Hold your horn up and even a little bit high. All of them do that. You never see a New Orleans musician point his horn to the ground and play down on the ground. That I can recall. Maybe there were some, but I just can't recall them right now. They all play with their horns straight out, aiming that tone out there so it's bouncing off a wall 40 feet away. Or going out in the thin air if you're playing a parade. The guys that didn't do that were the guys that didn't sound so good. Like this... I remember that's what Eddie Pearson said. Eddie Pearson always pointed his horn way out. And the other guy used to play with Eddie Pearson. He played with Paul Barber. He's a big, heavy set guy with a... He was a lot of sliding and stuff. Kind of a brassy, not really a real jazzy trombone player. Turbulon, I guess that was his name. Clemon. Yeah, he'd aim his horn down. Like... Yeah. With kind of bad hair, you know. But that's about the only thing I can say about holding the instruments. Aiming the horns up. Helps your playing. I mean that way I think you can get your singing. I think you can get the singing, aiming your horn down on the floor. Get the singing quality of it.
What about half-valving though? That isn't legitimate. How some of them do that?

Oh no. He was talking just about the way he was holding it. Yeah. Well this... You see now a valve instrument, a trombone player, he can do all sorts of little things. Lissandos because he's got a slime and a valve instrument doesn't. And these are where the real subtlies involved in the music. And I think it would take a young guy playing. I work on that half-valve stuff all the time because I think that's where you can get the real shadings and the meanings and the blues. Anything can play. Lee Collins... I think Lee Collins playing with the Astoria Hot 8 on that Label X. And those are available in quite a few other 45s and things. It's some of the best examples on record of using your valves for different sounds. Half-valves and stuff. It really comes through. Every little thing... When he ends a phrase, he can end it on a half-valve or he bends it. Louie did a lot more of that than he used in the past and he does now.
I noticed the D does a lot of that with his lip too, not just with his... Yeah.

It's a combination of lip and valves on that. You bend notes. As a matter of fact, I never thought when I'm trying to play that I should hit it right on a button. You know? Hit it above or below to get that bending quality. That gives you the blues sound. A Negro scale has been graphically illustrated as flatting the 3rd and the 7th. You know? But actually it's every note. A Negro scale is so completely African in nature that it hasn't any relationship to a diatonic scale. At first, here it says that's what gives the music so much rough quality to it. You say rough, you can't figure it out. You say, well it has a rough sound but yet they're not playing ragged. You know? When I say ragged, I mean when they hit, hit, start off, well not starting off the tune. Because they do start off tunes kind of raggedy now and then. But when they got it down where I saw a guy who go one, two, and then they whap, they hit it. They all hit it together. But it's the rough quality of the horns. And that rough quality is hitting a note above or below to get that blues sound.
What about somebody like Punch who's traveled a lot and been away more or less since the 20s? Do you think it changed his philosophy or his style?

Oh yeah, I think it changed Punch a lot. I think Punch from the records that I've heard of Punch is so completely different than what he plays now. He wouldn't know it was the same guy. I mean even the tone. I wonder, I'm just curious if that's what would happen to all normal musicians if they had to go and travel and play with different styles of bands. But the guys that were really solid, all the good bands and the whole history of jazz music had some New Orleans men in them affecting that band. From Duke Ellington to-
You know the Al Cooper, Savoy, Sultans had a New Orleans drummer in them.
Yeah.
Bands like that, I don't know if you heard of them, but all the modern guys rave about that.

Yeah, I never heard of myself. I believe that the New Orleans influence on music in America never be overly stressed. And I've heard some guys saying, well, jazz started everywhere, it just didn't start in New Orleans. But everything seems to refute that. The bands that were really showed the way, the ones that were the most significant bands had New Orleans men in them. And it wasn't just an accident that they were in the band either. Well listen to Henderson before, Louie, and after they were in the band. Absolutely. That was a pretty good example. Yeah, right.
Perfect.

Changed the whole band. Yeah. So when somebody like Sammy Price says that jazz started in New York, it's ridiculous because the record's refuted. The Henderson band before Louie was so stiff. Well, it didn't sound to me any different than a white man practically. It's part of the tonality, you know.
Well even a band like Paul Whiteman, you can feel the difference in the rhythm when you hear the bass player.

Steve Brown. Right. Another New Orleans man. Every band had had anything the same. Yeah. Yes sir, I can go along 100%. Maybe we'll stop this time. Yeah, that's everything I wanted to say anyway. I just want to bring out the individual thing. Jim Robinson on Climax Ray. Unless Ed's got something else. We've got a minute to do. If you think of anything Ed, do you want to ask if it still kind of bothers you?
Yeah. That is the whole idea of the school is to perpetuate an art form. Do you think it's still possible?
Through white musicians.

Well it's obvious. I don't think you can do it with color. It's like that old question. I don't think the younger color ones will want to. Well it's obvious it's going to have to be divorced from the environment that first posted this music. Do you think it can still be done?

Yeah, to a point. Like I say it'll never be exactly the way the guys did it. No, I don't think no matter how hard a guy tries it just can't. You'll never have quite that. It's undefinable because it's there but you don't know what it is that makes their music just a little bit more distinct than a band assimilating the style. From just the musical angles. It's a way of life. That way of life no longer exists. Therefore you're not going to have the music exactly like the way it was. I'm afraid that's it.

But really it hasn't been the end of it. How did you say that? How did you say that? How did you say that? How did you say that? How did you say that? How did you say that? How did you say that? How did you say that?

segments.chapter: Teaching New Orleans style
segments.title: Opening of the recording at American Music Records
segments.summary: Dick Allen opens the recording at Donald Russell's record shop on July 4, Armstrong's birthday, and introduces the plan for a New Orleans jazz school.

segments.chapter: Teaching New Orleans style
segments.title: Starting a band by ear: simple blues, chords and parts
segments.summary: DeVore explains how to get beginners playing: take melody and chords off records, start with a blues and simple parts for piano, trombone, clarinet and cornet, and learn chords as Johnny Wiggs showed him.

segments.chapter: Teaching New Orleans style
segments.title: Classical training of the New Orleans men and the Arban book
segments.summary: He says New Orleans players often had real classical training, citing Kid Thomas and Manuel Perez's markings in the Arban book; Allen asks if all should learn piano.

segments.chapter: Teaching New Orleans style
segments.title: Discipline, starting from a model, and brass band influence
segments.summary: Modern players struggle with the discipline of the style; DeVore discusses the Pee Wee Irwin George Lewis imitation, choosing a model, Jelly Roll's band-style piano and brass band roots.

segments.chapter: Rhythm, phrasing and tone
segments.title: Four-four rhythm and getting punch
segments.summary: Allen asks how players get the New Orleans rhythm; DeVore says four-four and punch matter more than notes.

segments.chapter: Rhythm, phrasing and tone
segments.title: Phrasing, attack and tonality defined
segments.summary: They define the three things DeVore's bass player says make jazz feeling: phrasing, attack and tonality.

segments.chapter: Rhythm, phrasing and tone
segments.title: White and Black players and the beat; Doc Evans's advice
segments.summary: DeVore says white players land on the beat and Black players play against it, recalling Doc Evans telling him to play off the beat; Allen compares clapping on one and three.

segments.chapter: Rhythm, phrasing and tone
segments.title: Phrasing off the beat and vibrato as tonality
segments.summary: DeVore describes playing ahead of or behind the beat, Armstrong and Oliver, and how vibrato gives the hot tone.

segments.chapter: Rhythm, phrasing and tone
segments.title: Ending-of-phrase vibrato and trombone slide vibrato
segments.summary: They discuss cracking vibrato at the end of phrases, clarinet and cornet vibrato, and how trombonists like Jim Robinson and Louis Nelson use lip and slide.

segments.chapter: Band building and learning from musicians
segments.title: Teaching by band versus individual lessons
segments.summary: Allen asks how to start the school; DeVore favors the band setting because of collective improvisation.

segments.chapter: Band building and learning from musicians
segments.title: Basic drum and bass parts for beginners
segments.summary: DeVore outlines simple drum parts (bass drum four-four, press rolls on two and four) and bass playing tonic and fifth, never a third on a strong beat.

segments.chapter: Band building and learning from musicians
segments.title: Paul Crawford as teacher and the basic band setup
segments.summary: They plan to use Paul Crawford to teach, and DeVore says the blues in different tempos is the first step for a band.

segments.chapter: Band building and learning from musicians
segments.title: Guest lecturers: New Orleans musicians sitting in
segments.summary: DeVore explains how visiting players such as Jim Robinson or Kid Thomas could teach tone and phrasing by playing with a student band.

segments.chapter: Band building and learning from musicians
segments.title: Getting along in a band; Albert Warner and Sonny Henry
segments.summary: DeVore says a band with bad feeling cannot play well, and mentions the unspoken closeness of Albert Warner and Sonny Henry.

segments.chapter: Band building and learning from musicians
segments.title: Lessons that are just talking; musicians DeVore learned from
segments.summary: DeVore says lessons can be talk about life, and names Kid Punch, Kid Thomas, Manuel Perez and Johnny Wiggs as the trumpet men he spent most time with.

segments.chapter: Band building and learning from musicians
segments.title: Pride and confidence of the New Orleans musicians
segments.summary: DeVore describes the tremendous pride and love of music beneath Jim Robinson's clowning and the other New Orleans men.

segments.chapter: Climax Rag and tempo and meter
segments.title: Jim Robinson's trombone part on Climax Rag
segments.summary: On the second reel, DeVore tells how Jim Robinson, after a Sunday session on July 1, sang the missing trombone part of Climax Rag to Rusty; they mention the earlier record.

segments.chapter: Climax Rag and tempo and meter
segments.title: Slow tempos and the importance of the drummer
segments.summary: Prompted by Kid Thomas's remark that they played too fast, DeVore says New Orleans bands play moderate dance tempos and that drummers who drag can ruin a band.

segments.chapter: Climax Rag and tempo and meter
segments.title: Sense of meter and whether it can be learned
segments.summary: They discuss meter as something learned in childhood, with examples of Ed singing, DeVore's wife and a classically trained piano player who jumped meter.

segments.chapter: Ensemble, harmony and the Ory band
segments.title: Silence, holes and ensemble integration of the front line
segments.summary: DeVore explains leaving holes in the lead so clarinet and trombone can fill in, contrasting New Orleans with Dixieland, Kid Thomas and Doc Evans, and the discipline this requires.

segments.chapter: Ensemble, harmony and the Ory band
segments.title: Harmony in the band: Oliver and Jelly Roll arrangements
segments.summary: Asked about harmony, DeVore discusses breaks and harmonized parts in the Oliver band and the polished Ory band with Mutt Carey.

segments.chapter: Ensemble, harmony and the Ory band
segments.title: Mutt Carey and the Kid Ory band
segments.summary: Allen and DeVore praise Mutt Carey's tonal shading, vibrato and phrasing, and talk about Ory as a demanding trombonist and bandleader.

segments.chapter: Ensemble, harmony and the Ory band
segments.title: Harmony parts, rough ensemble and arranged New Orleans music
segments.summary: They discuss loose harmony choruses, George Lewis's band as an intermediate style, Doc Evans's quartet-like harmonies, and Oliver and Jelly Roll arrangements.

segments.chapter: Ensemble, harmony and the Ory band
segments.title: Ory's discipline with modern players
segments.summary: Allen recalls an Ory interview about reading parts; DeVore says Ory gets his sound even from modern musicians.

segments.chapter: Minneapolis band and favorite players
segments.title: DeVore's Minneapolis band, audiences and Wild Bill Davison
segments.summary: DeVore says his band has won a Minneapolis following by rhythm and just enough music, rivaling Doc Evans, and praises Wild Bill Davison's attack, tone and phrasing.

segments.chapter: Minneapolis band and favorite players
segments.title: Jim Robinson versus Honore Dutrey as trombonists
segments.summary: Asked whom he prefers, DeVore picks Jim Robinson for his punch, while saying Dutrey had a nice style and was gassed in World War I.

segments.chapter: Technique, New Orleans influence and the school's future
segments.title: Holding the horn and fingering in New Orleans playing
segments.summary: DeVore says New Orleans players aim the horn up and out, mentioning Percy Humphrey's fingering and Eddie Pearson.

segments.chapter: Technique, New Orleans influence and the school's future
segments.title: Half-valving, bending notes and the blues scale
segments.summary: They discuss half-valve effects, Lee Collins's records, and hitting notes above or below for the blues sound.

segments.chapter: Technique, New Orleans influence and the school's future
segments.title: How travel changed Punch Miller
segments.summary: Allen asks whether travel changed Punch; DeVore says Punch's playing is now very different from his early records.

segments.chapter: Technique, New Orleans influence and the school's future
segments.title: New Orleans influence on jazz everywhere
segments.summary: They argue that the important bands had New Orleans men, citing Fletcher Henderson before and after Armstrong and Whiteman's bass player.

segments.chapter: Technique, New Orleans influence and the school's future
segments.title: Can the New Orleans tradition be perpetuated by a school?
segments.summary: Ed Lewis asks whether the art form can survive; DeVore says only partly, since the way of life is gone, and the tape closes.
